title: Recollections of an Ifugao ambush
summary: This is the story of how then-young governor Gualberto 'Bert' Lumauig braved the trauma and continued to serve — and be loved by his constituents — in Ifugao

blocks.text: BAGUIO, Philippines – I was five years old when my father, Governor Gualberto “Bert” Lumauig, was ambushed. We were living and studying in Quezon City. I remember visiting him in Veterans Hospital, where his room was cordoned off from media and guests, allowing only immediate family members inside his room. The ambush was on the headlines for days. Hundreds of telegrams of well-wishes were sent to him. Flowers and gifts were not allowed at all, apparently for security purposes.

I admired my Mom for her strength, ensuring Dad was cared for. Asking her years later how she took in all the violence that transpired, losing Uncle Jake and Uncle Peping, and leaving my Dad badly scarred. She said she held on to her faith and the utmost support of family and friends. Mom went with Dad during his six-month rehabilitation in the United States, but also made sure that we, their seven rambunctious children (ranging from ages 14 to 5), were left with able members of the family (a long list of aunts and uncles plus our grandparents).

July 23 every year thereon became a solemn day for the family, a day of quiet remembrance for the deaths of two people very close to Dad’s hearts: Uncle Jake and Uncle Peping, and surviving a violent attempt on our Dad’s life.

July 23, 1970. Bert Lumauig, who had just turned 37 years old, was the young governor of Ifugao. He presided over a meeting at the Banaue Hotel, a project he spearheaded which was scheduled to be inaugurated in two days. After dinner he, together with executive secretary Jake Dugyon, proceeded back to the capital town of Lagawe, about an hour’s drive from Banaue.There was a vehicle escort traveling ahead of them. Feeling exhausted, he slumped on his side at the back seat. Jake was on his left looking drowsy himself. Sergeant Manolo Domingo, his lone security, was seated directly in front of him beside his cousin Jose “Peping” Bacani, who was behind the wheel.

It was pitch dark and a bit foggy when they climbed up the driveway from the hotel to link up with the national road. They barely traveled two kilometers away from the hotel and negotiating a road bend when a volley of gunfire pierced the night’s silence and bullets rained on their car.

Instinctively he slid down from his seat to the floor. He tried to pull down Jake with his left arm but immediately stopped when bullets all but severed his arm. Jake moaned “Lord,” then pitched forward against the front seat’s backrest.

Gunfire continued without let-up. Bullets peppered his heavily padded winter jacket. He desperately fought to stay conscious and, as he did so, he thought he saw the likeness of the Virgin Mother and, from the depths of his heart, he whispered over and over the “Memorare,” the prayer his mother taught him in his youth.

He drifted back and forth from consciousness and unconsciousness, remembrances flashing like water in an onrushing stream that dropped in an eddy and whirled at no fixed direction, tears swelling his eyes as he asked what wrong had he committed against his people to deserve this barbaric attempt on his life. On their lives.

Gunfire seemed unstoppable. Bullets grazed his two ribs, a grenade shrapnel was embedded in his upper right head, and his upper right arm and back were bleeding. He managed to slowly crawl out of the left car door, weak but emboldened until he collapsed in a water-filled deep canal along the road.

Raul Casumpang, interpreter of the local Court of First Instance in Lagawe, was rushing to Banaue that night in his private jeep to visit a seriously ill relative. He met the speeding escort and was told about the ambush. Himmediately mobilized residents of the nearby sitios to come to their rescue. Upon reaching the ambush site, governor Lumauig was not in his car, so Casumpang walked a few distances until he came upon the governor’s helpless body profusely bleeding on the canal.

Casumpang rushed the governor to the nearby Good News Clinic and Hospital, a non-stock, non-profit religious mission hospital in Tam-an, Banaue. In and out of consciousness, governor Lumauig remembered pleading to the doctor and nurses, “Please do not cut off my arm,” as he seemed to feel his left arm dangling from the extensive bullet wounds, hanging by the cartilage and flesh.

“Try not to speak, Sir,” said the doctor, who he learned later was Dr. Romulo Emlano. Assisting him were two young ladies, one from Mayoyao, Norma Bongyo (who would later become his goddaughter in marriage when she got married to provincial engineer Sarol of Banaue), and Florence Cayong, from Banaue.
“The others, Jake, Manolo, Peping,” he weakly repeated.
“Sir, you’re badly wounded,” was the reply he got from Dr. Emlano.

He could hear calls for blood donors since he was losing so much blood. Rushing to his bedside was then-barangay captain Juan Tillay. He offered to donate all his blood just so the governor would be saved. He also refused to leave the clinic, fearing that the gunmen would somehow return, knowing the governor had survived.

His eyes became heavy, thinking of his wife Felicisima and the kids. He hoped none of his people would exact “revenge” and touch off a bloodbath in his beloved province. Then he drifted into a deep sleep.

Seeing the severity of the injuries and without much equipment in the clinic, Dr. Emlano immediately suggested for the governor to be airlifted to Manila. It was late at night and the possibility of flying was impossible, so at the break of dawn governor Lumauig was flown from the Good News Clinic to Veterans Hospital in Quezon City, where he underwent surgeries amid security concerns. His left arm was saved, but it was badly scarred, and he lost any sensory abilities on the lower arm and fingers.

It was only days later that he learned that his executive secretary, Jake Dugyon, a model family man and devout Christian, and his cousin-driver, Peping Bacani, did not survive the ambush. Sergeant Domingo sustained bullet wounds in his legs and was immediately treated.

The extent of the governor’s injuries required him to undergo further medical procedures in the United States, where he spent six months of surgeries, physical rehabilitation, and psychological therapy. It was only upon his return to the Philippines when Banaue Hotel — a project he envisioned, tirelessly secured resources for and steadfastly pushed for its successful completion — was finally inaugurated.

Upon his return to Banaue, he made sure that he visited the Good News Clinic and Hospital to personally express his extreme gratitude to Dr. Emlano, the nurses, and staff for saving his life. Throughout the years thereafter, he championed GNCH’s work, from procuring medicines through Manila-based pharmaceutical firms to encouraging philanthropic partners to invest in the clinic’s mission.

Led by then-Criminal Investigation chief Colonel Ernesto Cariño, the ambush was thoroughly investigated. It was discovered that there were seven foxholes in the ambush site, plus 75 empty shells of varied high-powered automatic rifles and two grenade safety pins.

There were also empty sardine tin cans and bread wrappers, indicating the ambushers were prepared for a long wait to accomplish their killing mission. There were arrests made, where one gunman confessed and named the alleged mastermind behind the dastardly deed.

Then-President Ferdinand Marcos offered the governor to join the diplomatic service with an ambassadorial position, perhaps with the assumption that the ambush had discouraged governor Lumauig from seeking another political term. He respectfully requested the President to allow him to consult his local leaders. The President agreed, and even invited him to bring the leaders to Malacañang.

The governor brought his trusted advisors Eladio Malingan, Santiago Habawel, Santiago Balajo, Jose Guinid, Amado Bokiagon, and some of the mayors. In the audience with the President, they were vehement in their objection to governor Lumauig leaving the leadership of Ifugao.

Despite veteran political personalities out to ease him out, Lumauig trounced his rival for governor with an avalanche of votes by the grateful people of Ifugao, appreciative of his performance and service. He went on to became assemblyman and congressman of Ifugao, selflessly serving his beloved province for another two decades.

I had thought that the ambush was already behind him decades later, especially after noticing that he was no longer hiding his ugly scars on his left arm, wearing short sleeve polos in public. But when he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s dementia in 2016, one of his nightmares in the middle of the night was dark memories of that fateful night in 1970. While I was by his bedside, he would start shouting repeatedly, “Protect your Mom, there are men after us!” I had to assure him that Mom was quietly sleeping beside him.

The progression of his dementia caused traumatic memories of the ambush to re-emerge, making events from decades ago seem vividly present once again. These moments that made me scared, upset, and melancholic. I knew things would get worse than better, but at the same time I had to remain optimistic for his sake.

Eight years ago on November 18, 2018, we lost our Dad. He had been in and out of the hospital for years, and his physical body just gave up. From that ambush in 1970 where his left arm was shattered, to his Parkinson’s disease where his right hand had uncontrollable tremors, and progressing to dementia where traumatic memories creeped on him relentlessly, we had to accept that his time on earth was up, and that God needed another angel in heaven. – Rappler.com

The author based most of the narrative of the ambush on the book Into the New Horizon: Ifugao, written by her father, the late Gualberto “Bert” Lumauig, published in 2008. A reprint will be available soon.

Good News Clinic and Hospital, which remains the only hospital in Banaue, Ifugao, is fighting to continue its mission too. It is raising funds through a sale of donated artworks until December 6, 2026.
